proof.text: Flatness makes multiplication by $0\ne s\in V$ injective on $A$: tensor the injection $V\xrightarrow{s}V$ with $A$. Thus $A\hookrightarrow A_K$. Integral closure is a subring containing $A$. Every intermediate ring $A\subseteq D\subseteq A_K$ is $V$-torsion-free, hence flat by [lem-trf-valuation-torsionfree-flat]. If $D$ is finite type over $V$, choose $P=V[X_1,\ldots,X_r]\twoheadrightarrow D$. Applying [lem-trf-valuation-finite-type-module-presentation] to the cyclic $P$-module $D$ gives a finite free presentation $P^m\xrightarrow{U}P^n\xrightarrow{q}D\to0$ [def-sc-finitely-presented-module]. To check the cyclic kernel explicitly, lift $1_D$ to $v\in P^n$, and lift the images of the basis vectors under $q$ to a row $r:P^n\to P$. If $J=\ker(P\to D)$, then $1-r(v)$ and the finitely many $r(U(e_j))$ lie in $J$. For $x\in J$, $xv\in\operatorname{im}U$, so $x=x(1-r(v))+r(xv)$ lies in the ideal they generate. Thus $J$ is finitely generated and $D$ is finitely presented as a $V$-algebra. If moreover $D$ is a finite $A$-module, the same lemma with $V\to A$ and $M=D$ gives finite presentation as an $A$-module. These observations will apply to each finite intermediate algebra below. The zero algebra satisfies the conclusion. If $V=K$ (height zero), then $B=A$ and the assertions follow directly.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, Step 3 and Lemma 3.5.1, printed pp. 20–23; valuation presentation tool: Stacks 053E(2); primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: We first establish reduced geometric fibres of the relative integral closure, without assuming it finite. For a prime $\mathfrak q$, integral closure commutes with localization by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-commutes-localization], so $B_{V\setminus\mathfrak q}$ is the integral closure of $A_{V\setminus\mathfrak q}$ in $A_K$. For $\mathfrak q=0$ it equals $A_K$. For $\mathfrak q\ne0$, put $W=V_{\mathfrak q}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak qW$, $E=B_{V\setminus\mathfrak q}$ and $k=W/\mathfrak m$. The residue field $k$ is separably closed by the first clause of [lem-trf-sepclosed-valuation-geometric-components]. It is also perfect: if its characteristic is $p>0$, lift any $c\in k$ to $W$, choose $0\ne t\in\mathfrak m$, and take a root in $K$ of $X^p+tX-c$: in equal characteristic $p$ its derivative is the nonzero constant $t$; in mixed characteristic $K$ is algebraically closed because a characteristic-zero separably closed field has no algebraic extension. A root is integral over $W$ and hence belongs to $W$ (a valuation ring is integrally closed: a root of negative valuation makes the leading term of a monic equation have uniquely least valuation). Its residue is a $p$th root of $c$. In characteristic zero perfection is immediate. A perfect separably closed field is algebraically closed, since every irreducible polynomial is separable.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, end of Steps 3–4 and opening paragraph of §4, printed pp. 23–24; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: If $a\in E$ satisfies $a^n\in\mathfrak mE$, write that membership as a finite sum and choose a nonzero $x\in\mathfrak m$ dividing all its scalar coefficients; valuation ideals are linearly ordered, so $a^n\in xE$. The value group of $W$ is divisible by [lem-trf-separably-closed-value-group-divisible], hence choose $y\in\mathfrak m$ with $x/y^n\in W^\times$. Then $(a/y)^n\in E$, so $a/y$ is integral over $E$. Transitivity [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive] and the definition of $E$ as a relative integral closure imply $a/y\in E$. Thus $a\in\mathfrak mE$, proving $E/\mathfrak mE$ reduced. The residue field is algebraically closed by the preceding step, so [lem-trf-geometric-reducedness-algebraic-closure-test] makes this fibre geometrically reduced. For $\mathfrak q=0$ use the assumed geometric reducedness of $A_K$. The affine fibre and reduced-ring comparisons [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] and [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-reduced-iff] identify these scheme assertions with the tensor products in the item. Every map $V\to\Omega$ to an algebraically closed field factors through the fraction field of $V/\ker(V\to\Omega)$, so all its claimed fibres are covered.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, final paragraph of Step 3 and Step 4, printed p. 23; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: For height one choose $0\ne\pi\in\mathfrak m_V$; $K=V[1/\pi]$. Write hats for $\pi$-adic completion. The formal comparison [lem-trf-valuation-rank-one-formal-comparison] gives the algebraically closed analytic field $\widehat K$, the flat topologically finitely presented model $\widehat A$, and the reduced affinoid algebra $C=\widehat A[1/\pi]$. Apply [lem-trf-valuation-grauert-remmert-powerbounded] to the image of $\widehat A$ in $C$ to obtain finitely many generators $z_i$ of $C^\circ$ over $\widehat A$. This remains valid when $C=0$. Finite-module integrality [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral] shows that $C^\circ$ is integral over the image of $\widehat A$. Conversely an element integral over this bounded image is power-bounded: its monic recurrence expresses all powers in the span of finitely many initial powers with bounded coefficients. Thus $C^\circ$ is exactly the relative integral closure of the image of $\widehat A$ in $C$.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, Steps 2–3, printed pp. 22–23; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Write $z_i=\widehat a_i/s_i$ with $s_i$ a power of $\pi$ and $\widehat a_i\in\widehat A$. The projection $\widehat A\to A/\pi^NA$ is surjective, restricts to the quotient map on $A$ and has kernel $\pi^N\widehat A$ [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-mod-power]; so choose $a_i\in A$ with $\widehat a_i-a_i\in s_i\widehat A$. Replacing $z_i$ by the image of $a_i/s_i$ changes it by an element of the bounded model, so it still lies in $C^\circ$ and these new elements still generate $C^\circ$ as an algebra over the image of $\widehat A$. A monic equation for the image of $a_i/s_i$ yields, after clearing denominators and using that the flat $\widehat V$-algebra $\widehat A$ has no $\pi$-torsion and so embeds in $C$, $a_i^m+c_1a_i^{m-1}s_i+\cdots+c_{m-1}a_is_i^{m-1}\in s_i^m\widehat A$. Approximate the $c_j$ by elements of $A$ modulo $s_i^m\widehat A$; this inclusion is preserved. The scalar saturation clause of [lem-trf-valuation-rank-one-formal-comparison] then puts its left side in $s_i^mA$. Dividing the resulting equality in $A_K$ gives a genuine monic equation over $A$ for $a_i/s_i$. Put $D=A[a_1/s_1,\ldots,a_r/s_r]\subseteq B$. A finite list of integral generators makes $D$ finite over $A$: monomials with exponents below their monic degrees span. Step 1 makes $D$ flat finitely presented over $V$ and finitely presented as an $A$-module.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, Step 3, printed pp. 22–23; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: The finite-module completion clause of [lem-trf-valuation-rank-one-formal-comparison] identifies $\widehat D\subseteq C$ with the $\widehat A$-algebra generated by the images of $a_i/s_i$, namely $C^\circ$. Let $b\in B$ and write $b=a/s$ with $a\in A\subseteq D$ and $0\ne s\in V$. Its image in $C$ is integral over the image of $\widehat A$, so it belongs to $C^\circ=\widehat D$. Hence the image of $a$ belongs to $s\widehat D$. Scalar saturation for $D$ gives $a\in sD$; writing $a=sd$ and using torsion-freeness in $A_K$ gives $b=d\in D$. Thus $B=D$, proving finiteness for height one. This reasoning does not assume $A\to\widehat A$ injective and also handles components on which $\pi$ is a unit.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, Step 3, printed p. 23; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Now induct on a finite height $h>1$. Valuation primes form a chain, so there is a minimal nonzero prime $\mathfrak p$; $V_1=V_{\mathfrak p}$ has height one and $W=V/\mathfrak p$ has height $h-1$. Put $T=V\setminus\mathfrak p$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(W)=V_1/\mathfrak pV_1$, which is separably closed by [lem-trf-sepclosed-valuation-geometric-components]. By localization of integral closure [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-commutes-localization] and the height-one result, $B_T$ is finite over $A_T$. Choose finitely many generators, clear their $T$-denominators to get $b_i\in B$, and put $A'=A[b_i]$. Their monic equations make $A'$ finite over $A$ and step 1 makes it flat finitely presented over $V$. We have $A'_T=B_T$, relatively integrally closed in $A_K$ by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive]. Transitivity also shows that the integral closure of $A'$ in $A_K$ is still $B$.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, Step 4, printed p. 23; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-valuation-finite-height-composition] to $A'$ and $\mathfrak p$. It gives $\mathfrak pB=\mathfrak pA'$ and identifies $B/\mathfrak pB$ with the relative integral closure of $\bar A=A'/\mathfrak pA'$ in $F=A'_T/\mathfrak pA'_T=\bar A\otimes_WL$. The algebra $\bar A$ is flat finitely presented over $W$: reduce a finite presentation, and for an injection of $W$-modules its tensor product with $\bar A$ is the same as tensoring those $V$-modules with $A'$, hence remains injective. Its generic fibre $F=B_T\otimes_{V_1}L$ is geometrically reduced by steps 2–3. The induction hypothesis therefore gives finite generation of $B/\mathfrak pB$ as a $\bar A$-module. Lift module generators to $c_1,\ldots,c_l\in B$ and include $1$. For every $b\in B$ subtract an $A'$-linear combination of the $c_i$ representing its residue. The difference lies in $\mathfrak pB=\mathfrak pA'\subseteq A'$. Thus $1,c_1,\ldots,c_l$ span $B$ over $A'$. Since $A'$ is finite over $A$, multiplying the two finite spanning lists proves $B$ finite over $A$. This completes the finite-height induction.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, Step 4, printed pp. 23–24; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: For arbitrary height, [lem-trf-valuation-arbitrary-height-limit] gives $K_0\subseteq K$, the finite-height valuation ring $V_0=V\cap K_0$, and $A_0$ with $A=A_0\otimes_{V_0}V$. Apply the finite-height result to the relative integral closure $B_0\subseteq A_0\otimes_{V_0}K_0$. Put $D=B_0\otimes_{V_0}V$. It is finite over $A$ by tensoring a finite spanning list. It is flat over $V$ since an injection of $V$-modules remains an injection as $V_0$-modules and tensoring it with $B_0$ preserves injectivity; tensor a finite presentation to get finite presentation over $V$. Its geometric fibres are reduced by [lem-trf-geometric-reduced-fibre-locus-base-change] and the affine fibre comparisons. Flatness embeds $D$ into $D_K$, and $D_K\cong (B_0)_{K_0}\otimes_{K_0}K\cong A_K$. The resulting inclusion $A\subseteq D\subseteq A_K$ makes $D\subseteq B$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral]. We have constructed a finite model; we have not assumed that integral closure commutes with this base change.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, valuation-limit portion of Step 5, printed p. 24; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: To identify this model with the relative integral closure, use [lem-trf-geometrically-reduced-eta-normal] for $\operatorname{Spec}D\to\operatorname{Spec}V$. The base is normal integral affine: a valuation ring is integrally closed by the monic valuation argument in step 2, its localizations are valuation rings, and affine schemes are qcqs. Flatness follows from [lem-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map-iff-flat-affine]; a finite algebra presentation gives a finitely presented affine morphism by the definition [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Let $b\in B$ and write $b=d/s$ with $d\in D$ and $0\ne s\in V$. The ring $D[b]\subseteq A_K$ is finite over $D$ because $b$ already satisfies a monic equation over $A\subseteq D$. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}D[b]\to\operatorname{Spec}D$ is finite by [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] and proper by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-proper]. It is an isomorphism on the generic fibre and on $D(s)$, since $b=d/s$. These opens are schematically dense on both schemes: localization at $s$ injects on their rings and on localizations of their rings, as both sit in the $K$-algebra $A_K$. Hence this is a finite $\eta$-modification, and the eta-normality lemma makes it an isomorphism. Consequently $b\in D$. This proves $B=D$, hence finiteness in arbitrary height.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, valuation-limit portion of Step 5 together with Proposition 3.5.2, printed pp. 20–24; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: We have proved $B$ finite over $A$, so it is finite type over $V$. The torsion-free and cyclic-polynomial-module arguments in step 1 now give flatness and finite presentation over $V$. Since $A\subseteq B\subseteq A_K$, localization at all nonzero elements of $V$ gives $A_K\subseteq B\otimes_VK\subseteq A_K$, with injectivity from torsion-freeness; the canonical map is an isomorphism. Steps 2–3 prove every required geometric fibre reduced. This proves all clauses without a nonemptiness or finite-height assumption.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5, valuation case of Steps 3–5, printed pp. 23–24; primary PDF read online, archival copy WANTED.

title: Relative integral closure over a separably closed valuation field
statement: Let $K$ be a separably closed field [def-kun-separably-closed] and let $V\subseteq K$ be a valuation ring with fraction field $K$: for every $x\in K^\times$, either $x\in V$ or $x^{-1}\in V$. Let $A$ be a flat finitely presented commutative $V$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map] [def-weil-pbc-finitely-presented-algebra]. Suppose $A_K=A\otimes_V K$ is geometrically reduced, meaning that $A_K\otimes_K E$ is reduced for every field extension $E/K$; reduced means having no nonzero nilpotent element. Regard $A$ as a subring of $A_K$. Put $B=\{b\in A_K: b\text{ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in }A\}$. Then $B$ is a finite $A$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], $B$ is a flat finitely presented $V$-algebra, the canonical map $B\otimes_V K\to A_K$ is an isomorphism, and $B\otimes_V\Omega$ is reduced for every homomorphism $V\to\Omega$ to an algebraically closed field. The valuation may have arbitrary height. The zero algebra is allowed.
